question: Which statement best describes Iframe basics?
options: The allow attribute sets a permissions policy controlling powerful features inside the frame — camera, microphone, geolocation, fullscreen, autoplay, payment. By default many of these are denied to cross-origin frames; you opt in explicitly (e.g., allow="fullscreen; autoplay"). This is how embed providers (YouTube, Stripe) request just the capabilities they need.

Every <iframe> should have a descriptive title attribute. Screen readers announce the iframe by its title ("Map of our office, frame"), so without one users hear something useless like 'frame' or the raw URL. The title is the iframe's accessible name — treat it as required, just like alt on an image.

sandbox locks down what the framed document can do: with an empty sandbox attribute it can't run scripts, submit forms, navigate the top page, or access its own origin. You then re-enable only what you need with tokens like allow-scripts, allow-forms, or allow-same-origin. Granting allow-scripts AND allow-same-origin together can let the frame remove its own sandbox, so combine them carefully for untrusted content.

An <iframe> ('inline frame') embeds an entirely separate HTML document inside the current page via its src. The framed page runs in its own browsing context with its own DOM and (usually) its own origin. Common uses are embedding maps, YouTube videos, payment widgets, and third-party tools. Give it width/height (or CSS) and remember its content is isolated from your page's scripts unless same-origin.

loading="lazy" defers loading an offscreen iframe until the user scrolls near it, saving bandwidth and speeding initial page load — important because embeds (maps, videos) are heavy and often pull in lots of third-party code. Use it for below-the-fold embeds; keep above-the-fold ones eager (the default) so they're ready immediately.

question: Which statement best describes The sandbox attribute?
options: Iframes cut both ways. Others framing YOUR site can trick users into clicking hidden buttons (clickjacking) — defend with the X-Frame-Options or CSP frame-ancestors header. YOU framing untrusted content risks it running scripts, navigating your page, or phishing — defend with sandbox, a tight allow policy, and only embedding trusted sources over HTTPS. Cross-origin frames are isolated by the same-origin policy, which limits but doesn't eliminate risk.
